subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Confirmation Bias in Action
description: A micro-lesson that makes Confirmation Bias in Action usable.

hook.text: An investor loved a stock and only read bullish articles. He ignored five warnings that predicted the crash.

buildup.text: Confirmation bias makes us seek evidence that supports what we already believe and skip the rest.

discovery.text: Wason's card test showed people verify rules instead of trying to disprove them. We test to confirm.

twist.text: Social media amplifies this. Algorithms feed you content you agree with, creating invisible echo chambers.

climax.text: Force yourself to seek one strong counterargument before every decision. Disconfirmation is a discipline.

punchline.text: The evidence you avoid is the evidence you need.

quiz.question: What does Wason's card test reveal?
options: People naturally seek to disprove rules
People seek to confirm rules rather than disprove them

details.summary: Confirmation bias in action describes how people seek, interpret, and remember information that confirms their existing beliefs while ignoring or discounting contradicting evidence. Once a belief forms, the evidence-gathering process becomes systematically one-sided.
details.whyItMatters: Confirmation bias is the most pervasive and damaging cognitive bias because it corrupts the evidence base for all subsequent reasoning. It makes strong opinions feel well-supported even when the supporting evidence has been selectively curated.
takeaways: People actively seek information that confirms existing beliefs
Ambiguous evidence is interpreted as supporting the preferred conclusion
Contradicting evidence is scrutinized more harshly than confirming evidence

faq.question: Why is confirmation bias so hard to overcome?
faq.answer: It operates at every stage of information processing: what you look for, how you interpret what you find, and what you remember. Each stage independently filters toward confirmation, creating a triple-layered bias that feels like objective analysis.

faq.question: What is the most practical defense against confirmation bias?
faq.answer: Actively seek disconfirming evidence before making a decision. Ask what would change your mind, then look specifically for that evidence. Assign someone the devil's advocate role. Reward people who surface contradicting information.
